asBirthCard.p: This one comes from your birthdate alone. Add up every digit of the date you were born and yours came to sixteen exactly. It's an uncomfortable-looking card to be handed, I know. Lightning takes the top off a tower and two people are falling out of it. Have a look at where it sits in the run of Majors, though. Just before it is The Devil, fifteen, where two people stand chained and could slip the chains off if they tried. Then sixteen, where the thing that held them gets knocked down whether they were ready or not. After it comes The Star, a woman kneeling by water at night, finally quiet. The card belongs to Mars, the planet of heat and force and the ruler of Aries and Scorpio, and it gets its temper from there. Whatever signs are in your own chart, people with this number tend to carry a bit of Mars around with them.

Mostly it shows up as a low tolerance for things that are quietly wrong. At a family dinner where everyone's stepping around the obvious thing, you're the one who ends up saying it, usually over dessert, and then there's a silence you could stand a spoon in. In a meeting where a plan is being nodded through, you've already spotted the number that doesn't work, and it bothers you physically to sit on it. When a friend sends a long text explaining why everything's fine with the new boyfriend, you read it twice and can tell it isn't. With a mechanic or a builder you want the bad news first and in plain words, and someone softening it just makes you suspicious.

You're often the best person to have around in the first hour of a real emergency. The pipe bursts at two in the morning, a parent gets rushed to hospital, the shop's been broken into, and while everyone else is still saying they can't believe it, you're already under the sink finding the stopcock and ringing the insurer. That's the Mars in this card, a planet that's at its best when something needs doing fast. And you don't need things to go back to how they were, which frees you up a lot. A friend whose business has folded gets a very practical conversation from you about what's still standing and what could be sold, and oddly that's the one that makes them feel better. You'll happily sit with them at the kitchen table and write out an actual list.

Plenty of people with this card don't complain as they go, and that's where most of the damage comes from. The flatmate leaves dishes, the manager keeps moving the deadline, your partner forgets the thing again, and you say nothing, week after week, because it doesn't seem worth the fuss. Then one ordinary Tuesday it all comes out at once, six months of it, and the other person is standing there genuinely shocked. To them it came out of nowhere. It didn't, of course. But they never got to hear the small version, back when a quick word would have sorted it, and by the time you do say something you've usually already decided, so there's nothing left for them to fix.

When something goes badly wrong, your first move is usually to act, and act hard. You resign the same afternoon, block the number, tell your brother exactly what you think of him, put the flat on the market. For a day or two there's real relief in it. A week later it lands in the body, bad sleep, a jaw that aches from clenching, a short fuse in the supermarket queue. That's usually also when you start wondering whether the whole thing needed burning down. Meanwhile your partner, or a kid who liked the old flat, is living with a decision nobody asked them about. What helps is putting something physical between the shock and the decision. A long run, a swim, an afternoon digging out the back garden. Do that first, then make the phone call, and wait until the next morning to send anything in writing.

You tend to want the real thing early. Somewhere around the third date you ask a question most people save for month six, about the ex, the family, what they actually want from their life, and some people find that thrilling and some quietly leave. Once you're in, you're very loyal to anyone who's been through a collapse with you. The partner who stayed when the job went, or gave up a whole weekend to help you move out of a flat at no notice, has you for good. The difficulty comes in the calm years. When nothing's going wrong you can start testing things, picking at a small crack to see if it holds, and a partner who likes things steady can feel they're always being checked. It helps to tell them straight when you're restless, so they know it's your mood and has little to do with them.

You're often at your best in work where things break and someone has to fix them. Emergency departments, IT outages, the building trade, crisis comms, a business turnaround, a restaurant kitchen on a Saturday night. You're also good at the unpopular part of any project, the audit, the post-mortem, the review where somebody has to say the software isn't working and they'd be better off starting again. Where it goes wrong is slow, polite organisations where the problem everyone knows about gets discussed for eighteen months. You can find yourself either blowing it up in a meeting or quietly handing in your notice, and neither does your reputation much good. Sixteens often change careers once in a big way, usually in their thirties, and the second one tends to fit better. If you're stuck somewhere slow, put your hand up for whichever project is in the most trouble.

A lot of sixteens have had the ground pulled out from under them at least once by twenty. A family breaks up, a course or a first job goes wrong in a spectacular way, the first big relationship ends with a revelation. It can leave a young person braced, half expecting the next one. Through the twenties there's usually some self-inflicted demolition as well, walking out of things that only needed a hard conversation. By the mid-thirties most people with this card have been through two or three of these and can tell a structure that's actually rotten from one that's just annoying them. The fifties tend to bring out The Star, the card that comes next. People with this number often get quieter around then, and end up as the friend others ring when their own roof falls in, because they know what the morning after actually looks like.

When you feel pressure building about something and you haven't said it yet, write it on a sticky note in five words or fewer, 'Sam keeps cancelling on me', and stick it inside the kitchen cupboard door. You'll see it every time you get a mug out. Once there are two notes up about the same person or the same job, that's your cue to raise it, calmly, within the week. Take the notes down after you've had the conversation.
